title: Pekudei: an open account (Exodus 38:21)
hook: Moses gives a public account of every gift, though no one asked

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one Shabbat labor with its own verse: kindling fire. Your line was no fire today. Did you catch a spark before it caught? Today, the last portion of Exodus. Day three hundred seventy-three.

A shared pot of money is a fragile thing. A group gift for a coworker, a family fund for a grandparent's care, the treasury of a club. And somewhere, someone is quietly wondering where it all went. Exodus has spent chapters collecting gold, silver and bronze from an entire people. Now the final portion begins, and before the sanctuary is even put together, Moses does something no one in the text has asked him to do. He publishes the books.
screen: `A SHARED POT OF MONEY.` → `WHERE DID IT ALL GO?` → `MOSES PUBLISHES THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Pekudei means the accounts, or the things counted, and the portion opens, in the JPS 1917 translation: "These are the accounts of the tabernacle, even the tabernacle of the testimony." Then come the numbers. So many talents of gold. So many talents of silver, and the Torah shows its work: the silver came from the half shekel, a half shekel from each man counted, six hundred three thousand, five hundred fifty of them. Remember half makes a whole? Here's where those half coins went. Then the bronze, and exactly what each metal became: sockets, hooks, the altar, the basin. In the text, nobody demands this. A midrash imagines why Moses did it anyway. It says some people were whispering behind his back, wondering whether the treasurer was getting rich. So Moses said: when the work is done, I'll give you an account. The same midrash adds a tender detail. Moses couldn't remember what one thousand, seven hundred seventy-five shekels of silver had been used for, and he was upset, until he looked up and saw them: the hooks on the pillars. The Mishnah carries this idea into later Temple practice. The officer who took coins from the Temple's collection chamber went in wearing clothes without folds or pockets, so no one could ever suspect him. A person, the rabbis said, should be clear in the eyes of people, just as in the eyes of God. Even Moses, who had spoken with God on the mountain, opened the ledger.
screen: `PEKUDEI: THE ACCOUNTS.` · `THE HALF SHEKELS, COUNTED.` · `WHISPERS, AND A LEDGER.` · `CLEAR BEFORE PEOPLE AND GOD.` · then, large: `ACCOUNT FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one place to be more open. Settle, and breathe. Think about where someone trusts you with something: money, time, a promise, a secret, a shared job. Is there anything there you've been vague about? A receipt never shared, a plan never explained, a delay never mentioned. Don't scold yourself. Just see it. Then picture laying it out plainly, the way Moses laid out the gold and the silver. Notice how much lighter that feels. The bell holds the time.
Pekudei. The accounts. The last portion of Exodus opens with Moses giving an open record of every gift.
Your line: account for it. Today, be transparent about one thing someone has trusted you with, before they have to ask. Day three hundred seventy-three.

screen: `DAY 373 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PEKUDEI: AS THE LORD COMMANDED.`

howItsDone: Jewish law and custom stress transparency for those who handle communal funds, and the Mishnah's description of the Temple treasury officer is often cited as the model.

fork.setup: you're Moses, the leader of the camp. you've collected gold and silver from everyone, and nobody has formally asked for an account. what do you do?
options: trust that your reputation is enough.
publish exactly how much came in and what it became.
let the priests keep the records privately.
fork.reveal: these are the accounts of the tabernacle: every metal, every weight, and what it became. even Moses opened the ledger.

original.note: Hebrew: the accounts, or the things counted, the first key word of the portion.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of numbers to skim.
what it means: Moses accounts publicly for every gift, down to the hooks on the pillars.

what a scholar hears: Shemot Rabbah 51 imagines the whispers and the forgotten 1,775 shekels; Mishnah Shekalim 3:2 grounds the officer's pocketless clothes in Numbers 32:22, be clear before God and Israel.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed the unsourced superlative 'the most trusted man in the camp' (teach and fork); the hook no longer tells the listener what is in their life; half shekel per man made explicit.
Exodus 38:21 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm wording.
603,550 men (38:26) and 1,775 shekels for the hooks (38:28): checked against the text; confirm.
Midrash on whispers about Moses and the forgotten 1,775 shekels: Shemot Rabbah 51:6 / Tanchuma Pekudei 7; confirm references and details.
Mishnah Shekalim 3:2: the officer entered without a cuffed garment, shoes, tefillin or amulet, citing Numbers 32:22; 'clothes without folds or pockets' is a simplification; confirm.
